presentingComplaint: Progressive symmetrical leg then arm weakness with unsteadiness over 6 days, now with breathlessness and difficulty swallowing.
history: Known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) followed in hepatology clinic, on spironolactone, furosemide and lactulose, with prior mild grade-1 hepatic encephalopathy that always resolved with lactulose titration. He had a self-limiting diarrhoeal illness about 2 weeks ago. Over the last 6 days he noticed tingling in the feet and hands followed by symmetrical, ascending weakness: first difficulty climbing stairs, then difficulty rising from a chair, and in the last 48 hours weakness of the hands, mild slurring, and nasal regurgitation of fluids. Today he feels short of breath lying flat. He denies fever, headache, neck pain or bowel/bladder incontinence. The referring team initially treated him as decompensated cirrhosis with encephalopathy and up-titrated lactulose, but sensorium remained clear and weakness progressed, prompting neurology review. No recent variceal bleed, no new sedatives, no missed lactulose doses.
examination: Alert, fully oriented (GCS 15) with no asterixis and no fetor hepaticus, arguing against active encephalopathy. Mild scleral icterus and moderate ascites consistent with his cirrhosis. Neurological exam: symmetrical flaccid weakness, MRC grade 3/5 proximally and 4/5 distally in the lower limbs, 4/5 in the upper limbs, with globally absent deep tendon reflexes and flexor plantars. Mild bilateral facial weakness and reduced palatal movement with a weak cough; single-breath count reduced to 15. Glove-and-stocking reduction in pinprick with preserved higher functions. No sensory level, no spinal tenderness, no fatigable ptosis or ophthalmoplegia. Resting tachycardia with labile blood pressure suggesting autonomic involvement.
imaging: MRI whole spine with contrast: no cord compression, no intramedullary or extramedullary mass, no enhancing cord lesion; incidental gadolinium enhancement of anterior spinal nerve roots and cauda equina. CT head: no intracranial mass or haemorrhage. Chest radiograph: low lung volumes with basal atelectasis, no consolidation.
microbiology: Not applicable (non-infective diagnosis). Prior stool studies during the diarrhoeal prodrome not available; serum anti-ganglioside (anti-GM1/GD1a) antibodies sent, result pending. Blood cultures negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating / axonal polyradiculoneuropathy) - favoured by post-diarrhoeal prodrome, ascending symmetric areflexic weakness, bulbar and respiratory involvement, albuminocytologic dissociation and nerve-root enhancement
Hepatic encephalopathy (decompensation confounder) - considered given cirrhosis, but clear sensorium, absent asterixis, near-normal ammonia and focal neuromuscular signs argue against
Spinal cord compression - excluded by MRI; no sensory level or sphincter disturbance
Myasthenic crisis - no fatigability, ptosis or ophthalmoplegia, reflexes lost rather than preserved
Metabolic encephalopathy from electrolyte/uraemic causes - normal renal function, electrolytes near normal, preserved cognition
finalDiagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) with early bulbar and respiratory involvement, in a patient with background alcohol-related cirrhosis whose hepatic disease mimicked but did not explain the deficit.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Guillain-Barré Syndrome and Other Immune-Mediated Neuropathies
European Academy of Neurology / Peripheral Nerve Society - Diagnosis and Management of Guillain-Barré Syndrome, 2023
stewardship: Not applicable - Guillain-Barré syndrome is an immune-mediated post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy, not an active infection. No empiric antibiotics are indicated; antimicrobials would be inappropriate. Disease-directed therapy is IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) or plasma exchange, with IVIG generally preferred here as plasma exchange can transiently deplete clotting factors and worsen the coagulopathy of cirrhosis. Corticosteroids are not effective in GBS. Immediate priority is airway/ventilatory surveillance with serial bedside forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, cardiac monitoring for autonomic dysfunction, and VTE prophylaxis.
contraindications: Avoid plasma exchange as first line where feasible given cirrhotic coagulopathy (factor and platelet depletion); prefer IVIG
Check IgA level and hydration/renal status before IVIG (risk of anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency, thrombosis, volume overload in ascites)
Do not use corticosteroids as monotherapy - ineffective in GBS
Avoid sedatives/opioids that could mask respiratory failure or precipitate encephalopathy
Do not attribute the deficit to hepatic encephalopathy and escalate lactulose alone
edgeCases: Cirrhosis-related asterixis and confusion can masquerade as encephalopathy, but GBS presents with clear sensorium, areflexia and ascending weakness
Early GBS may have normal CSF protein in the first week (repeat LP if initial dissociation absent)
Autonomic dysfunction can cause life-threatening arrhythmias and labile BP independent of respiratory status
Respiratory failure can occur with SpO2 still normal - trend FVC/NIF, not oximetry
Thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy of cirrhosis raise LP bleeding risk - correct as needed
expectedMaiK: Ascending symmetric areflexic weakness with bulbar/respiratory involvement after a diarrhoeal prodrome and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation is Guillain-Barré syndrome; the cirrhosis is a confounder, and the immediate imperative is serial FVC/NIF monitoring for neuromuscular respiratory failure plus IVIG.
